title: the butter thief

segments.voice: Yesterday the gopis brought Yashoda their list, and one look at the butter thief's frightened face stopped the scolding. Your line was they can't keep scolding.

Early morning in Nanda's house. The servants are busy elsewhere, and Yashoda is churning curd herself, pulling the rope back and forth around the churning stick, her bangles moving, singing, the text says, about the things her little boy has done. Then the little boy arrives. He's hungry, he wants his mother, and he takes hold of the churning stick so she can't go on. She lifts him into her lap and feeds him. A perfectly quiet scene. It's about to fall apart.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNING, SINGING.` → `HE GRABS THE CHURNING STICK.` → `A QUIET MORNING.`

segments.voice: On the fire, the milk starts to boil over. Yashoda sets Krishna down mid-meal and runs to it. He's furious. He bites his lip, cracks open the pot of curd with a stone, slips into another room and eats butter in secret. Yashoda comes back to a broken pot and no child. She follows the trail and finds him on an upturned mortar, handing butter from the hanging pot to a monkey, glancing around in case anyone sees. She picks up a stick. He jumps down and runs, and she runs after him. The Bhagavata pauses to marvel: the one the yogis can't reach even with their minds is being chased around the yard by his mother. She catches him. He cries and rubs his eyes, smearing them. She drops the stick and decides to tie him to the mortar instead, so he'll stay put. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width. She adds another. Still two fingers short. Every rope in the house, always two fingers short, and the neighbor women laugh, and so does she. She's sweating now, flowers slipping from her hair. Krishna sees how tired his mother is, and then, the text says, he lets himself be tied. Nothing in the universe can hold him. A tired mother's love can, because he allows it. Tradition says this is where one of his names comes from: Damodara, the one with a rope around his waist.
screen: `THE MILK BOILS OVER.` · `A BROKEN POT, A MONKEY, A STICK.` · `ALWAYS TWO FINGERS SHORT.` · then, large: `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has tried very hard for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, and picture them in the middle of that effort, a little tired, a little undone. Breathe in and see how much they were giving; breathe out and soften, the way Krishna softened at his mother's face. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.
Damodara. The name tradition gives Krishna for the rope at his waist, after he let his tired mother finally tie him.
Your line: he lets himself be tied. Tomorrow, two trees in the yard. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Krishna bound by Yashoda's rope is remembered in his name Damodara, and some Vaishnava communities honor this story in the autumn month of Kartika with songs and lamps offered to Damodara.

chat.says: How could Yashoda tie up Krishna if nothing in the universe can hold him?
options: Her rope was always too short until he saw her tiredness and let himself be tied.
She found a magic rope from the gods that was strong enough to hold him.
He was only a baby then, so he had no power yet to stop her.
chat.meaning: Every rope came up two fingers short. Seeing how tired she was, he allowed it: her love holds him because he lets it.
